problemText: Which of the following best describes what a synthesis essay requires a writer to do, distinct from a research report that simply surveys what several sources say?
choices: Select the single most persuasive source among those provided and restate its argument as the essay's own conclusion
Read several sources on one shared, debatable issue and build an original position that uses them as evidence
List each source's main point in turn and note where the sources agree or disagree, without committing to a stance
Summarize the historical background of each source's author before analyzing what the sources argue
hints: A synthesis essay is scored on the writer's OWN argument, not on how thoroughly every source got mentioned.
Rule out any option that never asks the writer to take a position of their own.

problemText: A writing task asks: "Read the two sources below on whether social media has been beneficial to teenagers, then write an essay that develops your own position, using the sources as support." A student instead plans to write one paragraph summarizing what each source says and a closing paragraph noting that people disagree. Which best explains why this plan fails the task as assigned?
choices: The plan fails because it skips a formal title page with full citations for both sources
The plan uses too few paragraphs to cover both sources, and the introduction falls short of the expected length
The plan quotes each source too many times, making the essay's use of evidence look disorganized to a reader
The task asks for the student's own defensible position; the plan only reports each source's content without ever taking a stance
hints: Compare what the prompt actually asks for ("develops your own position") against what the plan delivers (a report of two sources plus an observation that they disagree).
Noticing that sources disagree is not the same as arguing what that disagreement means.

problemText: A synthesis source is labeled: Source B, a city planner, writes, "Removing street parking to add bike lanes cuts local retail revenue within the first year." Which sentence in a student's essay correctly attributes and grammatically integrates this idea?
choices: As Source B's city planner warns, removing street parking for bike lanes "cuts local retail revenue within the first year," a cost that planners rarely mention up front
"Removing street parking to add bike lanes cuts local retail revenue within the first year." This proves bike lanes are bad policy for any city considering the change
According to Source A, removing street parking to add bike lanes cuts local retail revenue within the first year, a claim worth taking seriously
Removing street parking to add bike lanes is well known to cut local retail revenue within the first year, regardless of a city's specific circumstances
hints: Check three things: is the source named in a lead-in, is the quotation exact, and is it grammatically stitched into one sentence rather than standing alone?
One option credits the idea to the wrong source letter — watch the label carefully.

problemText: A student's draft reads: "Bike lanes reduce nearby retail revenue in year one. This shows bike-lane expansion needs a revenue-loss offset built into city budgets." The first sentence paraphrases a claim from Source B but never says so. Which revision best fixes the missing attribution?
choices: "Bike lanes reduce nearby retail revenue in year one." This shows bike-lane expansion needs a revenue-loss offset built into city budgets
Bike lanes reduce nearby retail revenue in year one, according to some studies that have looked into the issue over the past several years
As Source B's city planner reports, bike lanes reduce nearby retail revenue in year one — evidence that expansion plans need a built-in revenue-loss offset
It is often said that bike lanes reduce nearby retail revenue in year one, though no particular source is ever named for the claim
hints: Paraphrase needs attribution too, even without quotation marks — adding quote marks alone does not name a source.
Look for the option that names the specific source, not just a vague 'some studies' or 'it is said.'

problemText: A synthesis prompt provides: Source A: "Standardized tests give every applicant an identical, objective measure to be judged by." Source B: "Test-prep coaching that costs thousands of dollars means the 'objective' score mostly measures a family's bank account." Which thesis takes the most defensible position ACROSS both sources, rather than simply repeating one side?
choices: Source A argues standardized tests are objective, while Source B argues they are not
A test billed as an objective measure stops being one once unequal access to coaching lets wealth, not ability, decide the score
Standardized tests are the fairest tool available for judging every college applicant on equal footing
Whether standardized tests are fair or unfair depends entirely on one's perspective on the issue
hints: Apply the strip test: remove the source references from each option — does a real, arguable claim survive?
Rule out any option that only restates what one source says, and any option that just names disagreement without taking a side.

problemText: A student's draft thesis reads: "Some people think homework helps students learn, and other sources think it just adds stress, so it really just depends on the student." Which revision converts this into a defensible, arguable position rather than a description of disagreement?
choices: Homework helps learning only when its length is matched to a subject's actual practice needs; past that point, it adds stress without adding retention
It is hard to say for certain whether homework helps or hurts, since reasonable people disagree about its value
Sources disagree on whether homework helps or hurts, and both sides make valid points worth considering
Homework has both benefits and drawbacks, as shown by the differing sources provided
hints: A defensible position commits to a claim a reader could argue against; "it depends" has no real opposite to push back on.
Look for the option that states a specific mechanism (what makes homework help vs. hurt), not just that both effects exist.

problemText: A student drafts: "Source A says urban gardens increase neighborhood property values. Source B also discusses gardens, noting that garden upkeep often falls on volunteer labor that eventually burns out. Both sources talk about community gardens." Which revision replaces this book-report paragraph with one that integrates both sources as evidence for a single claim?
choices: Source A discusses property values from gardens, and then Source B discusses volunteer burnout, so both angles are worth knowing
Urban gardens are a clear net benefit to neighborhoods because they increase nearby property values
Community gardens are a complicated issue that involves both benefits and costs for a neighborhood

Community gardens raise property values only as long as someone keeps tending them, so a value gain that Source A celebrates is fragile precisely because Source B shows the volunteer labor sustaining it tends to burn out
hints: The delete test: in a book-report paragraph, any sentence can be removed without weakening an argument, because there isn't one — look for the option where removing either source's detail would actually weaken the claim.
The winning revision states a claim first and then uses each source's detail to support that same claim, rather than narrating each source in turn.

problemText: A draft paragraph reads: "Source A reports that reducing lunch periods to twenty minutes doesn't affect how much food students eat. Source B reports that students who eat lunch in under twenty minutes make significantly more trips to the nurse's office with stomachaches. The schools have short lunch periods." Which revision most effectively integrates both sources as evidence for one claim, rather than narrating each source in turn?
choices: Both Source A and Source B examine twenty-minute lunch periods, one from a food-quantity angle and the other from a health angle
Rushed lunch periods clearly damage student health, as the spike in nurse visits shows

A twenty-minute lunch period may not shrink how much food students eat, but Source B's spike in stomachache visits suggests it changes how safely they eat it — the real cost isn't quantity, it's the body's ability to handle a rushed meal
Source A's finding about food quantity and Source B's finding about stomachaches are both relevant considerations for schools to weigh
hints: Look for the option that states one claim and uses BOTH sources' details as proof for it, rather than listing what each source found.
A paragraph that just says both findings are 'relevant' or 'worth knowing' has no claim of its own yet.

problemText: A student's thesis is: "A city's ban on single-use plastic bags succeeds only when paired with an affordable, accessible alternative." Which roadmap sentence for the essay's body paragraphs is organized by REASON rather than by source?
choices: This essay will first examine what Source A says about the ban, then what Source B says about it, and finally what Source C adds
The ban must first change habits at the point of sale, then survive the cost burden on low-income shoppers, and finally hold up against enforcement gaps that let large retailers ignore it
Paragraph one will cover the city council's report, paragraph two will cover the retailer survey, and paragraph three will cover the consumer interviews
This essay will look at several different viewpoints on the plastic bag ban before reaching a conclusion
hints: A by-reason roadmap names the logical steps of the ARGUMENT, not which source gets covered in which paragraph.
Organizing by source, even when the sources are named clearly, tends to collapse an essay back into a source-by-source summary.

problemText: A synthesis essay argues that food-delivery apps have reshaped small-restaurant economics. Paragraph 2 has just shown that delivery apps expand a restaurant's reach beyond its neighborhood. Which transition sentence best opens paragraph 3 by connecting to a NEXT REASON, rather than announcing a switch to a new source?
choices: That expanded reach comes at a cost, though, once the delivery platform's commission is subtracted from every new order it brings in
Turning now to Source C, which surveyed restaurant owners directly about delivery fees, a different picture emerges
As shown above, delivery apps expand a restaurant's reach beyond its neighborhood
Restaurants have used many different marketing strategies over the past decade to attract new customers
hints: A strong transition connects the reasoning of paragraph 2 to a new, escalating point — it does not announce which source is coming up next.
Rule out the option that just restates paragraph 2's point without moving the argument forward.

problemText: A synthesis prompt asks students to read three sources on whether cities should subsidize electric-vehicle charging stations, then develop their own position. A student's outline opens each body paragraph with "Source A says...," "Source B says...," "Source C says...," and never states what the student concludes from each. Which best explains why this outline will likely underperform on the synthesis task?
choices: It cites too few sources overall, since the prompt technically allows citing more than three sources if additional supporting evidence happens to be readily available to the writer
It organizes each paragraph around reporting a source rather than around the student's own claim, leaving the student's position implicit rather than argued
It fails to include a formal citation format noting each source's original publication date and author credentials
It quotes each source too briefly throughout, reducing the overall word count of the finished essay below what graders typically expect
hints: A synthesis essay is scored on the writer's OWN argument, not on how faithfully each source got summarized.
Ask whether a reader could state the student's thesis after reading only this outline.

problemText: A synthesis prompt provides sources on whether homework should be assigned over school breaks. A student drafts: "Sources disagree on this issue, and this essay will explain both sides before concluding that reasonable people can disagree." Which best diagnoses the flaw in this plan, at the level of the task itself rather than mechanics?
choices: The plan cites an even number of sources overall, and synthesis essays on this particular exam are supposedly graded down for using an even number of sources
The plan's final sentence is too short to serve as an adequate concluding paragraph on its own
The plan never signals which sources will be quoted directly versus paraphrased
The plan announces disagreement and stops there; it never commits to the student's own defensible position on the issue itself
hints: Noticing that sources disagree is not the same as arguing what that disagreement means.
Check whether the plan's closing move is a stance or just an observation about the sources.

problemText: A synthesis source is labeled: Source A, a nutritionist, writes, "School lunch reforms cut plate waste by a third within one year." Which sentence correctly attributes and integrates this claim?
choices: As Source A's nutritionist reports, school lunch reforms "cut plate waste by a third within one year"
"School lunch reforms cut plate waste by a third within one year." This proves every school should adopt the same reforms immediately
According to Source B, school lunch reforms cut plate waste by a third within one year
School lunch reforms are well known to cut plate waste by a third, regardless of what any particular study found
hints: Check three things: is the source named, is the quotation exact, and is it stitched into a sentence rather than standing alone?
Watch the source letter carefully — one option credits the claim to the wrong source.

problemText: A student's draft reads: "Extending library hours increases teen visits. This shows library funding should prioritize evening staffing." The first sentence paraphrases a finding from Source C but never says so. Which revision best fixes the missing attribution while keeping the sentence properly integrated?
choices: "Extending library hours increases teen visits." This shows library funding should prioritize evening staffing
Extending library hours increases teen visits, according to research conducted at some unspecified point over the past several years by an unnamed organization
As Source C's circulation data shows, extending library hours increases teen visits — evidence that funding should prioritize evening staffing
It is often observed that extending library hours increases teen visits, though no particular source is typically named for the claim
hints: Paraphrase needs attribution too, even without quotation marks.
Look for the option that names the specific source rather than a vague 'some research' or 'it is often observed.'

problemText: A synthesis prompt provides: Source A: "Later school start times let teenagers get more sleep." Source B: "Later start times force some working parents to find new before-school childcare." Which thesis takes the most defensible position ACROSS both sources, rather than simply repeating one side?
choices: Source A argues later start times help sleep, while Source B argues they burden working parents, so the two sources simply disagree with each other
Later start times should be adopted only if paired with a supervised before-school program that absorbs the childcare gap Source B identifies
Later school start times are clearly beneficial for every single student enrolled in every district, regardless of that district's particular circumstances
Whether later start times are good policy depends heavily on each individual's personal opinion about mornings and family scheduling
hints: Apply the strip test: remove the source references — does a real, arguable claim survive?
Rule out any option that only restates what one source says, or that only names the disagreement.

problemText: A synthesis prompt provides: Source A, a labor economist, writes that a 15-dollar minimum wage "raises earnings for the lowest-paid workers with only modest job losses in high-cost regions." Source B, also a labor economist, writes that the same policy "produces steep job losses concentrated among the least-experienced workers in lower-cost regions." Which thesis takes the most defensible position across both sources?
choices: Source A supports a 15-dollar minimum wage while Source B opposes it, so the two labor economists simply and irreconcilably disagree with one another
A 15-dollar minimum wage is unambiguously good economic policy nationwide, since Source A already confirms that it raises earnings for workers
Because two credentialed economists disagree, no defensible thesis about the minimum wage can realistically be written from these two sources alone

A 15-dollar minimum wage's effect depends heavily on regional cost of living, so a single national wage floor risks helping low-cost-region workers' earnings while pricing out their least-experienced peers
hints: Notice both sources are credible economists — the disagreement may reflect a difference in region rather than a simple right/wrong split.
Look for the option that reconciles the two findings by scope, rather than picking a side or giving up.

problemText: A student drafts: "Source A says composting reduces landfill waste. Source B also discusses composting, noting that many households find the process too time-consuming to maintain. Both sources talk about composting." Which revision replaces this book-report paragraph with one that integrates both sources as evidence for a single claim?
choices: Composting only cuts landfill waste in practice if it stays convenient enough that busy households keep doing it — the very obstacle Source B raises
Source A discusses landfill waste, and then Source B discusses time constraints, so both angles are worth knowing
Composting is a clear net benefit for any city that adopts it widely
Composting is a complicated issue that involves both real benefits and real drawbacks for a household to weigh before deciding whether to participate consistently
hints: A book-report paragraph can have any sentence removed without weakening an argument, because it never makes one.
Look for the option that states a claim first and uses both sources' details to support that same claim.

problemText: A draft paragraph reads: "Source A reports that a downtown bike-share program saw 40% of trips replace car trips. Source B reports that the same city's bike-lane network still has significant gaps outside downtown. The city has a bike-share program." Which revision most effectively integrates both sources as evidence for one claim, rather than narrating each source in turn?
choices: Both Source A and Source B examine the same bike-share program, one from a ridership angle and the other from an infrastructure angle worth noting
The bike-share program clearly and unambiguously reduces car trips citywide, as the 40% figure from Source A already shows on its own
The bike-share program's strong 40% car-trip replacement rate is likely capped by Source B's finding that bike lanes thin out beyond downtown, leaving suburban riders without a safe route to use it
Source A's ridership finding and Source B's infrastructure finding are both relevant considerations that are worth mentioning somewhere in the essay
hints: Look for the option that states one claim and uses BOTH sources' details as proof for it.
A paragraph that calls both findings merely 'relevant' or 'worth knowing' has no claim of its own yet.

problemText: A student's thesis is: "A city's composting mandate succeeds only when paired with accessible, low-cost bins for renters." Which roadmap sentence for the essay's body paragraphs is organized by REASON rather than by source?
choices: This essay will first examine what Source A says about the mandate, then what Source B says, and finally whatever additional detail Source C happens to add
The mandate must first overcome renters' lack of storage space, then survive the added weekly cost of a bin rental fee, and finally prove itself through early pilot-program results
Paragraph one will cover the city council's report, paragraph two the waste-hauler survey, and paragraph three the renter interviews in turn
This essay will look at several different viewpoints on the composting mandate before eventually reaching some kind of conclusion
hints: A by-reason roadmap names the logical steps of the argument, not which source appears in which paragraph.
Organizing by source tends to collapse an essay back into a source-by-source summary.

problemText: A synthesis essay argues that ride-hailing apps have reshaped late-night public transit ridership. Paragraph 2 has just shown that ride-hailing apps pull riders away from late-night bus routes. Which transition sentence best opens paragraph 3 by connecting to a NEXT REASON, rather than announcing a switch to a new source?
choices: Turning now to Source B, which surveyed transit riders directly about ride-hailing use, a different picture emerges
As shown above, ride-hailing apps pull riders away from late-night bus routes
Public transit agencies have tried many different strategies over the years to boost late-night ridership
That lost ridership compounds itself once transit agencies respond by cutting the very late-night routes riders still depend on
hints: A strong transition connects paragraph 2's point to a new, escalating point — it does not announce which source is next.
Rule out the option that just restates paragraph 2's point without moving the argument forward.
